title: Patel Brothers, India Grocers, and the Quiet Empire Building of Indian Grocery in America
excerpt: From a 20,000-square-foot anchor store in Florida to a former Big Lots in Ohio, Indian grocery chains are expanding at a pace that mirrors the diaspora's own growth — and they are reshaping how America shops for food.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Patel Brothers is expanding with a new 20,000-square-foot store in Florida.
  • India Grocers is moving into suburban areas, reflecting demographic shifts.
  • Truly Indian has launched over 1,300 products since May 2024, tapping into the U.S. market.
  • Indian food is the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America.
  • The expansion of Indian grocery stores signifies a cultural infrastructure for the diaspora.

In St. Johns County, Florida, Patel Brothers is building a 20,000-square-foot grocery store on 4.25 acres at the Shops at Racetrack Road. In Dublin, Ohio, India Grocers is renovating a former Big Lots space on Sawmill Road. In Edison, New Jersey, a company called Truly Indian has quietly expanded to over 1,300 stores nationwide with frozen samosas, tandoori naan, and high-protein roti wraps. None of these stories made the front page. None of them trended on social media. But taken together, they tell a story that every NRI in America can feel in their bones: the Indian grocery business is booming, and it is no longer content to stay in the ethnic aisle. ## The Patel Brothers Playbook Patel Brothers was founded in 1974 — the same year that the first wave of post-1965 Indian immigrants was settling into American life and discovering that nobody in their new country sold fresh curry leaves. What began as a single store has grown into the largest Indian grocery chain in the United States, with more than 50 locations nationwide. The new St. Johns County store, which will anchor a developing retail center, is the chain's second in Northeast Florida, joining an existing location on Baymeadows Road in Jacksonville. It will include a Patel's Fresh Kitchen serving prepared foods — a model the chain has increasingly adopted to capture the growing demand for ready-to-eat Indian meals. "At Patel Brothers, our mission is to bring the best ingredients from South Asia, right to your doorstep," the company's website reads. The mission hasn't changed in fifty years. The scale has. > **""At Patel Brothers, our mission is to bring the best ingredients from South Asia, right to your doorstep," the company's website reads."** ## India Grocers Goes Suburban In Central Ohio, India Grocers is making a different kind of statement. The chain is moving into a former Big Lots property — one of several vacated by the discount retailer's 2025 closure — in Dublin, a suburb that has seen its South Asian population surge in recent years, driven largely by the tech corridor running through Columbus. The move is significant not because of the store itself, but because of what it represents. Indian grocery stores are no longer tucked into strip malls in explicitly ethnic neighborhoods. They are taking over anchor spaces in mainstream suburban retail corridors, competing for the same foot traffic as Kroger and Trader Joe's. ## The CPG Wave ![Sawmill Road — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/e/e3/SawmillRoad.jpg) While the brick-and-mortar chains expand, a parallel revolution is happening in packaged goods. Truly Indian, backed by ADF Foods — a global Indian food manufacturer founded in 1932 — has placed its products in over 1,300 stores since launching in May 2024. The lineup includes handmade frozen samosas (over 300,000 crafted fresh daily in India), verified low-glycemic tandoori and garlic naans baked in traditional clay ovens, and high-protein roti wraps marketed as "India's answer to the burrito." The pitch is deliberately dual-audience: authentic enough for the homesick NRI, accessible enough for the curious American. Indian food is now the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America, according to food data firm Dataessential, and the U.S. ethnic food market is estimated at $24.5 billion. ## Why Now? Three forces are converging. First, demographics: the Indian-American population has grown rapidly, concentrating in metros and suburbs that now have the density to support full-scale grocery operations. St. Johns County, Florida, and Dublin, Ohio, are exactly the kind of fast-growing suburban markets where Indian families are putting down roots.
Cultural Shift in Grocery Shopping
›Indian grocery stores are moving into mainstream retail spaces.
›Demographics show a growing Indian-American population in suburbs.
›Indian cuisine is now sought after by mainstream American consumers.
›Supply chains for Indian food have matured, ensuring quality and availability.
Second, mainstream crossover. Indian food is no longer exotic. It is the cuisine that Americans are actively seeking out — whether through fast-casual chains, Michelin-starred restaurants, or the spice aisle at their local Whole Foods. A generation of Americans has grown up eating tikka masala and naan, and they want to cook it at home. Third, supply chain maturity. Companies like ADF Foods have built the infrastructure to manufacture at scale in India and distribute reliably across the United States. The days of depending on a single importer with inconsistent stock are fading. The supply chain is professional, the cold chain is robust, and the product quality is high. ## The Diaspora Connection For NRIs, the expansion of Indian grocery stores is more than a business story. It is an infrastructure story — the infrastructure of belonging. When Patel Brothers opens in your suburb, it means you no longer have to drive an hour for fresh methi or the right brand of atta. It means your neighborhood recognizes you. It means home is a little closer. The fact that these stores are moving into former Big Lots and occupying anchor retail spaces is itself a marker of arrival. The Indian grocery store is no longer the scrappy newcomer. It is the tenant that landlords want. ## What's Next Expect the expansion to accelerate. Patel Brothers has been adding locations steadily, and the prepared-foods model gives it a revenue stream that pure grocery cannot match. India Grocers and regional chains are filling gaps in markets that Patel Brothers hasn't reached. And CPG brands like Truly Indian are betting that the grocery aisle — not the restaurant — is where Indian food will truly go mass market. The shelves are stocked. The aisles are widening. And somewhere, a first-generation immigrant who opened a tiny spice shop in 1974 is watching his grandchildren run an empire.
